title: Building a rectangle from a side of four and a diagonal of eight
description: A rectangle with one side of four centimetres and a diagonal of eight centimetres is built in the same order as before. The base goes first, then a perpendicular, then a compass arc for the diagonal.
teaching_notes: One idea: draw the known side as the base, raise a perpendicular at one end, and cut it with an arc whose centre is the other end of the base and whose opening is the diagonal. Watch for students who put the compass point on the wrong end.

video_script.why: A learner repeats the base, perpendicular and arc method with new lengths and checks the figure against the two rules of a rectangle.
video_script.substitution: the rectangle PQRS with the base PQ of four centimetres and the diagonal QS of eight centimetres
video_script.anchor: a rough rectangle PQRS with the base PQ marked 4 cm and the diagonal QS marked 8 cm
video_script.payoff_line: The rectangle is ready. Its sides are four centimetres and about six point nine centimetres, and its diagonal is eight centimetres.

final_answer.value: rectangle PQRS with PQ = SR = 4 cm, PS = QR about 6.9 cm and diagonal QS = 8 cm
final_answer.spoken: a rectangle with sides four centimetres and about six point nine centimetres, and a diagonal of eight centimetres

maths_rules: the base PQ is 4 cm and the line at P is perpendicular to PQ
S lies on that line and is 8 cm from Q, because the diagonal QS is 8 cm
the other sides PS and QR are equal, about 6.9 cm, since 8 x 8 - 4 x 4 = 48 and the square root of 48 is about 6.9
opposite sides are equal and all angles are 90 degrees
video_script.design: A rough rectangle PQRS stays at the side. The construction is drawn in four steps, and the compass opening of eight centimetres stays visible while the arc is drawn from Q.
